# The Open Mainframe: Why It's Becoming the Keystone of End-to-End Digital Enterprise Strategy

Mainframes never went away. But the way enterprises connect them to everything else is changing fast — and that shift matters more than most cloud-native teams realize.

## What's Actually Happening

The conversation around mainframes has quietly moved past the "lift and shift to cloud" narrative that dominated the last decade. Instead, enterprises are treating the mainframe as the keystone of their end-to-end digital architecture — not a legacy system to escape, but a foundational layer to integrate.

The Open Mainframe Project and broader open-source ecosystem have accelerated this shift. Rather than treating mainframes as isolated islands requiring specialized skills and proprietary tooling, organizations are bringing modern DevOps practices, open APIs, and standardized interfaces to these platforms.

This isn't about modernization in the traditional sense — replacing COBOL line by line or migrating workloads to AWS. It's about treating the mainframe as a first-class participant in the broader enterprise architecture. That means CI/CD pipelines that deploy to z/OS alongside Kubernetes clusters. It means observability stacks that pull telemetry from mainframe applications into the same dashboards as your microservices. It means security tooling that treats mainframe access with the same rigor as cloud IAM.

[UNVERIFIED] The Open Mainframe Project has seen significant growth in contributors and projects over the past several years, with initiatives like Zowe providing open-source frameworks for mainframe integration.

The practical outcome: teams that previously treated mainframe work as a separate discipline — different tools, different pipelines, different security models — are now unifying their approach. The mainframe becomes one node in the mesh, not a walled garden.

## Why the "Keystone" Framing Matters

Architecture metaphors get overused. But "keystone" is actually apt here.

A keystone isn't the biggest stone in an arch. It's the one that holds the others in position. Remove it and the structure fails. That's how mainframes function in most large enterprises — they process the transactions that everything else depends on. Banking core systems. Insurance claims processing. Airline reservations. Healthcare records.

The shift to treating mainframes as the keystone of end-to-end digital strategy acknowledges this reality instead of fighting it. Previous modernization approaches often tried to work around the mainframe or treat it as technical debt. The current approach says: this is load-bearing, so let's make it work better with everything else.

This has implications for how teams think about integration:

**Data flows become bidirectional.** Instead of batch exports from mainframe to data lake, you get real-time event streams. Mainframe transactions trigger downstream processes in cloud-native systems. Cloud applications write back to mainframe systems of record.

**Security models unify.** The mainframe has historically had its own identity and access management patterns — RACF, ACF2, Top Secret. Integrating these with enterprise IAM (OAuth 2.0, OIDC, modern identity providers) means one security model instead of two.

**Observability extends.** If your mainframe applications don't show up in your APM tooling, you have blind spots. Open mainframe initiatives are pushing for standard telemetry formats that let mainframe metrics live alongside everything else.

## Why Practitioners Should Care

If you're a developer or security engineer who doesn't touch mainframes directly, you might wonder why this matters to you.

Here's the thing: your systems probably depend on mainframes whether you know it or not.

That API you call for account balances? There's a decent chance it terminates on a mainframe. The batch job that populates your reporting database? Mainframe. The authentication flow for your enterprise app? Might pass through mainframe-backed identity systems.

When the mainframe is treated as a black box, problems happen:

**Incident response gets slow.** Something breaks, and half the team doesn't have visibility into the mainframe layer. You're waiting for a different group with different tools to investigate.

**Security gaps emerge.** If your SAST tooling doesn't scan COBOL, and your IAM doesn't integrate with RACF, you've got coverage holes. Attackers know this.

**Deployment coordination becomes painful.** You want to ship fast, but the mainframe release process runs on a different cadence with different approvals. End-to-end automation becomes end-to-almost-end automation.

The open mainframe movement addresses these friction points. Not by making everyone a mainframe expert, but by making the mainframe accessible through familiar interfaces.

Zowe, for example, provides a REST API layer that lets you interact with z/OS using standard HTTP calls. You can script mainframe operations the same way you script AWS operations. Your CI/CD pipeline can deploy to the mainframe using the same patterns it uses for your container deployments.

This doesn't eliminate the need for mainframe expertise — someone still needs to understand CICS, IMS, and the underlying systems. But it removes the requirement that everyone on the team have that expertise just to integrate with it.

## The Security Angle

From an application security perspective, the open mainframe approach opens up possibilities that were previously impractical.

**Unified vulnerability management.** If your mainframe code lives in the same Git repositories and deploys through the same pipelines as everything else, you can apply the same security scanning. SAST tools are starting to support COBOL and PL/I alongside Java and Python. This means one vulnerability database, one triage process, one set of SLAs.

**Consistent access controls.** Integrating mainframe identity with enterprise IAM means you can enforce the same policies everywhere. No more separate approval workflows for mainframe access. No more orphaned accounts because offboarding processes didn't include the mainframe layer.

**Audit trails that make sense.** When mainframe operations go through standardized APIs with proper logging, you get audit trails that your SIEM can actually ingest. This matters for compliance, but it also matters for incident response.

The risk, of course, is that opening up the mainframe also expands the attack surface. REST APIs that weren't there before become new targets. Integration points become new vectors. This is where the security engineering matters — you don't just expose everything; you do it with the same rigor you'd apply to any new service.

## What to Watch

Several trends will determine whether the open mainframe approach delivers on its promise:

### Skills and Adoption

The mainframe skills gap is real. The people who deeply understand these systems are retiring. The question is whether the open tooling makes the systems accessible enough that the next generation can maintain and extend them — or whether we're just adding API layers to systems that fewer and fewer people understand at a fundamental level.

Watch for: training programs, community growth around projects like Zowe, and whether enterprises are actually hiring for combined cloud/mainframe skills or still treating them as separate roles.

### Vendor Behavior

IBM controls much of the mainframe ecosystem. Their support for open-source initiatives matters. So far, they've been supportive of the Open Mainframe Project and contributed to tools like Zowe. But vendor behavior can shift.

Watch for: pricing models that encourage or discourage openness, proprietary lock-in tactics that undermine open APIs, and whether the open tools remain genuinely community-driven or become vendor-controlled.

### Security Maturity

Opening the mainframe means new attack surfaces. The security tooling needs to keep pace. This means SAST tools with solid COBOL support, API security solutions that understand mainframe integration patterns, and IAM products that handle the hybrid identity problem well.

Watch for: whether the security vendor ecosystem treats mainframe as a real market or an afterthought, and whether enterprises actually enforce consistent security policies across mainframe and cloud.

### Real-World Integration Stories

The concepts make sense. The question is execution. We need to see enterprises actually running unified CI/CD pipelines, unified observability, unified security — not just pilot projects or conference talks, but production systems.

Watch for: case studies with specifics, not just testimonials. What did they actually integrate? What broke? What did they learn?

## What to Do Next

If you're on a team that interacts with mainframe systems — directly or indirectly — here's a practical checklist:

**Map your dependencies.** Do you know which of your services depend on mainframe systems? If not, find out. Trace the APIs, trace the data flows, understand where the mainframe sits in your architecture.

**Talk to the mainframe team.** If your organization has a separate mainframe group, start a conversation. What's their current tooling? What are their pain points? Are they exploring open frameworks like Zowe? What would unified pipelines look like?

**Evaluate your security coverage.** Does your SAST scan mainframe code? Does your IAM integrate with RACF or equivalent? Does your SIEM ingest mainframe logs? Identify the gaps.

**Pilot something small.** If you're interested in better integration, don't try to boil the ocean. Pick one workflow — maybe a single API endpoint or a single deployment pipeline — and see if you can unify it. Learn from that before scaling up.

**Stay informed.** The Open Mainframe Project publishes updates on its various initiatives. If this space matters to your organization, someone should be tracking it.

## The Bigger Picture

The end-to-end digital enterprise concept only works if it actually includes everything end-to-end. For most large organizations, that means the mainframe.

The open mainframe movement represents a maturation of the industry's thinking. Not "how do we get off the mainframe" but "how do we make the mainframe work well with everything else." That's a more realistic question for organizations that have decades of investment and millions of lines of code running on these systems.

Whether this approach succeeds depends on execution, vendor cooperation, and skills development. The tools are emerging. The concepts are sound. The open question is whether enterprises will actually adopt them in production, or whether mainframes will remain islands despite the available bridges.

---

**For your team:** If you're in an enterprise with mainframe systems, how integrated are they with your modern development and security workflows — really? Not the strategy deck version. The actual reality.
